hints: Focus on what concentrated sulfuric acid does to an alcohol, think dehydration to form an alkene plus water.
Check each alcohol for how many different places the H can be removed from alongside the OH group to make a C=C bond.
Look for the alcohol that is unsymmetrical enough to give two different positions for the double bond, so two positional isomers form.
walkthrough:
**Recall the reaction type**

Great start, let's spot the reaction first. Concentrated sulfuric acid dehydrates an alcohol to an alkene.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$\text{alcohol} \xrightarrow{\text{conc. } H_2SO_4} \text{alkene} + H_2O$$

**Think about when two isomeric alkenes form**

To get two structural isomers, the OH must be on a carbon where removing H from the left side gives a different alkene from removing H from the right side. That needs an unsymmetrical secondary alcohol with different alkyl groups on each side.

**Test hexan-2-ol**

Look at $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. Remove OH from C2 plus H from C1 gives hex-1-ene, while OH from C2 plus H from C3 gives hex-2-ene. These are positional structural isomers, so this fits perfectly.

options.A: Hexan-2-ol is a secondary, unsymmetrical alcohol. Dehydration can place the double bond between C1-C2 to give hex-1-ene or between C2-C3 to give hex-2-ene. These two alkenes are structural (positional) isomers of each other.
options.B: Pentan-1-ol is a primary alcohol with OH on C1. The only H that can be removed to form C=C is from C2, giving only pent-1-ene. No second structural isomer is possible.
options.C: Pentan-3-ol looks promising because it is secondary, but it is symmetrical. Removing H from C2 or from C4 gives the same product, pent-2-ene. Only one alkene structure forms, so this is a classic symmetry trap.
options.D: Propan-2-ol dehydrates to give only propene, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CH}_2$. There is no other carbon position for the double bond, so no pair of structural isomers can form.
